# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it clearly worth it?

whys.g1: The three answers say different things (wanting a trial pair at a matinee first, needing it to catch audience questions in a big hall, and getting by with an end seat on the good side), so leaving each on its own is how I'd sort them and no group was forced.
whys.g2: There's no junk or explicit answer here, and Tomás's off-question workaround answer was left out of any group rather than counted as a reason it would be worth it.

founder.order_why: It runs context, then problem, then solution (what it is, fit, advantage, start-up), then who asks and who gets the link, which is how I'd explain AirCaps to someone new.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 show the identical kicker and question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.') on either side of the window screen, so the second one reads like the same question again even if it collects different context fields.
founder.missing: Nothing asks about money. There is no screen for the price ($599 glasses with free captions, or $20/month Pro, which is $599 to $839 a year), what wearers spend today on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, who pays (the wearer, HSA/FSA eligible, nobody else has to agree), or the commitment step (order the caption glasses with 15-day free returns). PRIMARY.missing: What I already do to keep up (lipreading, asking people to repeat, a captioning app on my phone, an interpreter) and how well that works, plus what AirCaps would cost.

screens.why4: The only chip is *I'm not sure*, which is the founder's escape the card allows, and a box of up to four lines of nine words is the right shape for my benefits.
screens.why5: My line "More of the talk followed without asking for repeats" sits in the box as I typed it, nine words, nothing changed.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 benefits of at most 9 words each, measured against today's way, with *I'm not sure* as the only escape; my one row is a noun phrase naming what changes, so it can carry the belief.
screens.instead: What would deaf or hard-of-hearing adults get in a fast or noisy conversation that today's way doesn't give them? One a line, up to four, e.g. "fewer times asking people to repeat".

screens.why1: Right after I typed what it does better, Keel shows back the benefit it will test, which is the obvious next check.
screens.why2: The meaning is mine, but 'more of the talk followed' is clunky, and in the belief 'would have given them more of the talk followed' needs a second read.
screens.why3: Following more of a conversation without making people repeat themselves is exactly what my wearers know from every table they sit at.
screens.why4: One row, one gain, no overlap, under 9 words, and it is the benefit I lead with.
screens.why5: It still says what I typed: following more without asking anyone to repeat.
screens.why7: The row is a single noun-phrase gain carried whole into the belief, but the belief says 'their last conversation' rather than the hard case, a group conversation that was too fast or too noisy, so the occasion is any conversation, not the one the advantage is for.
screens.instead: Row: 'Following more of the talk without asking for repeats'; belief: 'For most, with it, their last group conversation that was too fast or noisy would have let them follow more of the talk without asking for repeats.'

screens.why1: After the fit and the advantage, asking what wearers have to do to start using the glasses is the natural next question about my solution.
screens.why2: Setup, extra steps and learning, up to four and nine words each, is plain to me, and I answered at once in my own words.
screens.why3: I know exactly what a wearer has to do: put the glasses on for conversations and keep them charged.
screens.why4: A free box for up to four efforts with an 'I'm not sure' chip to leave the dimension out is the right control, and the escape fits.
screens.why5: Nothing is rewritten here; my two efforts stand as I typed them, and the next screen is where I check Keel's version.
screens.why7: The prompt draws out one to four efforts the wearer takes themselves, which my two rows are (wearing them in conversations as a new habit, charging daily), with 'I'm not sure' as the founder's escape the card allows.
screens.instead: What will they have to do themselves to start using it and keep using it (setup, learning, or a new daily habit)? Up to four, each up to 9 words.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they'd have to do to start, it's obvious Keel shows back the efforts it drafted before I pick one to test.
screens.why2: Wearing the caption glasses in conversations and charging them are how I and my users already talk about it, so I read it on first pass.
screens.why3: Both are efforts the wearer takes themselves and knows from their own week: putting the glasses on at the table, and plugging them in at night.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, the first-use habit and the upkeep habit, both in the wearer's words; nothing nonsense or overlapping.
screens.why5: My row is kept exactly, but *Charge the glasses every day* is Keel's addition with a daily figure I never typed (my material gives no battery life), and it sits in the list like one of mine.
screens.why7: Both rows are steps the wearer takes themselves on the one measure and stay off Compatibility's phone-online ground, but the second reads as Keel's suggestion shown as a plain row with no why, carrying a number that isn't mine, so the shape rule is bent.
screens.instead: Rows: *Wear the caption glasses in conversations* (picked) · suggested, last, with its why: *Pair the glasses with the app once* (a one-time setup before first use) -- or, if charging stays, *Charge the glasses most nights* marked as Keel's suggestion with its why.

screens.why1: Right after I checked my adoption-effort rows, picking the one effort strangers will be tested on is the obvious next step before the commercial section.
screens.why2: Both rows read plainly to me; caption glasses and charging them every day are how I talk about the product.
screens.why3: I know which effort trips up my wearers, and I chose wearing the glasses in conversations as the one most likely to stop them.
screens.why4: The two rows are separate efforts: my own row about wearing the glasses in conversation, and Keel's suggested daily-charging habit, which is a real friction for anyone getting through a day of conversations.
screens.why5: My row appears exactly as I revised it in r24, the belief repeats it word for word, and nothing is reworded.
screens.why7: The measure, shape and belief all fit: two efforts the wearer takes themselves, my row first, the suggested new habit last, picked row equals belief, and the 1-in-3 bar can go either way; but the screen does not show the suggested row's why or the founder-side *I'm not sure* chip the card allows.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? — Wear the caption glasses in conversations · Charge the glasses every day (suggested: a new daily habit for all-day wear) · I'm not sure

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the natural moment to decide whether to ask respondents to try the glasses for real, and I have a 15-day risk-free return offer ready to back it.
screens.why2: Pilot is a word any founder uses, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents will see and where I find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want early wearers' emails is my own call about my own launch.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this choice, and no escape is needed.
screens.why5: Nothing here drifts from what I typed, and the respondent's line names no product, price or role, so nothing leaks.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint says Keel records the voice while the picked answer talks of a face, and 'tap Saskia to hear her and switch' leaves unclear whether hearing her also switches to her.
screens.why3: I know my people well enough to pick an interviewer, and the hint answers my first worry: every question is written on screen and people can type or tap, so a deaf respondent is not shut out.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct and playable, but for deaf and hard-of-hearing adults I would want to know which face is easiest to lipread, or have a text-only or captioned-first choice, and neither is offered.
screens.why5: It names my people in my own words ('deaf or hard-of-hearing adults') and nothing of AirCaps or the glasses leaks to respondents.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Questions always show as text on screen. Options: Daphne (clear, lipreadable face) ▶ · Saskia ▶ · Text only, no video. 400 credits for a video interviewer.

screens.why1: Once I've picked who asks the questions, choosing how my respondents answer is the obvious next step before the study goes out.
screens.why2: AI interviewer, read and tap, and let them choose are plain to me, and each description says exactly what the respondent will do.
screens.why3: I know my wearers well: many are hard of hearing and many rely on text, so I can easily judge whether a spoken video interviewer or a read-and-tap form suits them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete as formats, but Daphne is pitched as asking questions aloud to people who can't follow speech, and Read and tap offers speaking into the box to people who may not speak clearly or at all, with no note that captions or text are the real channel for this audience.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps' product or roles leaks into the choice, and my pick, Read and tap, is kept.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? — Read and tap (read each question, tap or type the answer) / AI interviewer Daphne (every question shown as text on screen, with spoken audio as an extra; answer by typing or tapping) / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing how people answer, the obvious last step before sending is deciding who gets a link.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'Contacts page' is Keel's own page, explained in the option, and 'sign in with Google' is everyday.
screens.why3: I know whether I have named deaf and hard-of-hearing people to send to or a group like a HLAA chapter or Facebook group where I'd post one link.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real choices, but the open-link option's Google sign-in is a quiet hurdle for some older hard-of-hearing members of a community group and isn't flagged as optional.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles leaks, and my pick (people I know by name) still reads as I meant it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits under the title, the count line says all 3 beliefs hold, each card carries its deciding count against its bar (7 of 7 vs bar 5 of 7), and 'the verdict is the worst of all its cards' ties them together.
screens.why_b2: Each card says plainly what was counted (said yes / would have gone better / would do it), over how many (7), and where my bar sits (5 of 7), so I read it on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card beliefs and names are the ones I checked, but Keel's statement of my solution is garbled ('wearing the glasses an app on lightweight glasses shows live captions ... and gets back live captions ... inside the lens'), and the Relative advantage line is clumsy though recognisable.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what three holding beliefs mean for AirCaps or what I should do next; the only explanatory line describes the method, not the idea.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and nothing is called strong, but a unanimous 7 of 7 from only seven people is never flagged as a small sample, and the 3 who would wear the glasses only on a condition are still counted as 'would do it'.
screens.instead: State my solution in one clean sentence ('An app on lightweight glasses shows live captions of nearby speech inside the lens'), add 'only 7 people answered, so treat 7 of 7 as an early signal', name the condition the 3 put on wearing the glasses, and say what to do next, such as testing the price and the commitment step with these people.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip marks my bar at 5. All of it is plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and 'could read captions while watching faces' are the dimension and condition I picked. The asked clause is the one I wrote.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely that this condition won't be what stops the wearer and points me to Adoption friction as the thing to look at next.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly calls 7 people a lean, not a call, but the So line then says flatly that this 'is not what will stop them', which is a soft overstatement for a small group.
screens.instead: Say 'With 7 of 7 yes in a small group, reading captions while watching faces looks unlikely to be what stops them; Adoption friction, below, is the weaker point.'

screens.why_b1: 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said it would have gone better, 7 of them a lot · bar 5 of 7', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts 'better' over 7 people, splits it 7 a lot and 0 a little, and the strip puts my bar at 5 of 7 with its 1-in-3 rule, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: My benefit is there word for word, but the belief and question say 'their last conversation' and 'the most recent time you tried to follow and join a face-to-face conversation', not the group or noisy conversation that was too fast to follow, which was the hard case I checked.
screens.why_b4: It says all 7 imagined it going better and sends me on to Adoption friction to see whether they would actually wear the caption glasses, which is the real next question for a hardware product.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is said, but the question described AirCaps as 'an app' when it is caption glasses, so this 7-of-7 is about something I don't sell and reads stronger than the data can carry.
screens.instead: Ask about 'the last conversation with hearing people that was too fast or too noisy to follow', describe AirCaps as 'caption glasses that show what people say', and keep '7 of 7, a lean from a small group'.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know the belief held and the number that decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip shows 7 cells for me with the marker at 5, so all three things are plain at a glance.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the step I picked, in my words.
screens.why_b4: The So line says what would make it worth it to the 3 is below, but the notes below don't say that: Harriet wants a trial matinee, Ruth wants audience questions picked up, and Tomás describes his end-seat workaround. None of them speaks to comfort through a whole conversation, so I'm left to work out for myself that wearability and a try-before-you-buy are the next things to prove.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and the count line calls it a lean, not a call, so 7 of 7 is not oversold.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would wear them as is; 3 only if they stay comfortable through a whole conversation. Prove all-day comfort, and lean on the 15-day returns so people can try a pair at a real table or matinee before they commit.

screens.why_b1: The verdict and its deciding number sit together: 'Adoption friction held, 7 of 7' and '7 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 3 on a condition'.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Adoption friction and the belief line, 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations', is the revision-24 wording I checked.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what the three conditions mean for the launch, such as offering a trial pair through the 15-day returns or testing pickup of audience questions in large halls.
screens.why_b5: All three quotes carry the same condition, 'Only if it stays comfortable through a whole conversation', but none of them says it: Tomás describes a workaround that already works, Harriet wants a trial under stage lights, and Ruth wants audience questions picked up. The trailing 'for' adds to the confusion.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I did not type: a one-sided-deafness seating workaround that competes with the glasses, demand for a try-before-buy matinee under stage lights, and mic pickup of audience questions in big halls.

screens.why1: It's the first screen and it checks I'm someone who actually talks with hearing people, which the rest of the study is about, so it's obvious why it's asked first.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how deaf people talk about the hearing world, so the question is plain to me on first read or first hear.
screens.why3: I know whether I talk with hearing people every week; I do it at the shop, at work and with my family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it with no overlap, and a gate rightly has no escape chip.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment, 'talk with hearing people every week', and nothing about a product or the founder's terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question with two options a listener can easily hold, though the plainer 'Yes or no.' that §17 sets for a screener would sound less stiff than 'I'll read 2 options.'

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it's obvious the next thing is whether one of those conversations got away from me this week.
screens.why2: "Lose track of a conversation" is exactly how I'd say it: the moment you realise you've no idea what they're on about now.
screens.why3: I know straight away whether that happened to me in the last seven days; it's my own week, not a guess.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it, and the chips sit with the story box after a Yes, so they don't muddy the gate itself.
screens.why5: Nothing about any product or company reaches me; it's just my own conversations with hearing people, in words I'd use.
screens.why6: One short question with a plain "Yes or no" at the end; easy to take in once, even read on captions.
screens.why7: The gate asks the thing that goes wrong, not the weekly talking everyone in the group does: a week of quiet one-to-ones with good lipreading is a true No, and a noisy family dinner where I got lost is a true Yes, with no escape, as the card requires.

screens.why1: After asking whether I lost track of a conversation with hearing people this week, showing me an idea for captions in glasses is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses, lens and eye contact are all everyday words for me, and I'd get it on the first read.
screens.why3: Following conversations with hearing people, and looking down at a phone caption app instead of at their face, is my own week, so I can picture this straight away.
screens.why4: It's a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The product is named on purpose as an idea to imagine, the words are mine (captions, people nearby talking), and no founder jargon or role labels reach me.
screens.why6: It is short, plain sentences with no parentheses, slashes or abbreviations; saying 'lightweight glasses' and 'inside the lens' twice is a little repetitive aloud but easy to hold.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions inside the lens. While people nearby talk, you read what they're saying in the lens. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the glasses idea, asking whether I could read captions and still watch faces is exactly what I'd want to know first.
screens.why2: Captions, speakers' faces, last conversation: all plain to me, I read the question once and know what it means.
screens.why3: I never had caption glasses, so I have to imagine whether I could have read them and still caught faces and lips, which is partly a guess.
screens.why4: The four ability options cover it from easy to not at all without overlap, and I can't tell fits since I have never tried this.
screens.why5: The card says plainly what AirCaps is, and nothing of anyone's plan or labels for people leaks into the question.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and four short options said as a list are easy to hold, though for a deaf listener the AI voice itself is another matter.
screens.why7: It is an ability on the one measure (could I have), the four ability options are in order with the last two against, some of us could and some could not so it can hold or fail, and I can't tell is the only escape.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the captions-while-watching-faces question, it makes sense to ask whether those glasses would have helped me.
screens.why2: I'd just say I was talking with hearing people or trying to keep up, not that I 'tried to follow and join' a conversation, and 'done that better' leaves me working out which part is meant.
screens.why3: I talk with hearing people every week, so I can picture my last conversation and judge whether captions in my glasses would have helped.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and 'I can't tell' fits someone who has never tried captions on glasses.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks, but 'follow and join a face-to-face conversation' reads like their job line rather than how I'd put it, and the idea is cut down to 'an app' when the card said glasses.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, the stem runs past twenty words before the question, so I'm holding a lot before the four short options arrive.
screens.why7: The four options, their order and the separate escape are right, but the occasion is any recent conversation rather than one that was too fast or too noisy to follow, so a talk I handled fine pulls toward 'no difference'.
screens.instead: Think of the last time a conversation with hearing people was too fast or too noisy to follow. Would AirCaps, captions in your glasses, have helped you keep up better, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the reveal and the 'better or not' question, asking whether I'd actually put the glasses on is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Wearing caption glasses in a conversation is something I can picture and answer straight away, in words I'd use myself.
screens.why3: I know whether I'd wear glasses at the dinner table or the work meeting where I lose track, and how I feel about people noticing them.
screens.why4: The four answers run from yes to no without overlap, and the condition is the real one for me, whether it stays comfortable for a long conversation; 'I can't tell' fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own name and description reach me, and 'caption glasses' is how I'd say it, so nothing of the founder's plan or terms leaks.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question with four short answers I can hold and one escape said last.
screens.why7: The effort is one I take myself, wearing the glasses; the options are the fixed four in order, with the condition being my own assurance and not a fear, two for and two against, and 'I can't tell' apart.

screens.why1: After three questions about the glasses, it makes sense to ask in my own words what would make them worth having.
screens.why2: Short, plain words, and AirCaps was already named on the idea card, so I know what it means.
screens.why3: I know what I'd need from captions in a fast or noisy conversation, like keeping up, catching names and being right, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It uses only the name already shown on the idea card and adds none of the founder's own terms.
screens.why6: One short question, easy to hear once and answer out loud.
